intro: The unit of evidence matters: a whole program, a recorded encounter and one learner’s next sentence answer different questions.
unresolved: The card wording, retry, observer questions and stop rules are proposed teaching designs informed by the adjacent studies and guidance. Their effect on mutual understanding, coercion, readmission and length of stay is unresolved. Rodolico et al.’s 12-month schizophrenia relapse OR of 0.18 concerns family psychoeducation; the ≤2-session category showed no significant benefit. Do not carry an OR or NNT onto these cards.

citation.authors: Jacobsen RK, Sørgård J, Karlsson BE, Seikkula J, Kim HS
citation.title: “Open Dialogue behind locked doors” – exploring patients’, family members’, and professionals’ experiences with network meetings in a locked psychiatric hospital unit: A qualitative study

records.sample: 5 patients and 6 relatives (written accounts); 5 professionals (focus group)

notes: The two network leaders were nurses and social workers; the staff focus group was four psychiatrists and one psychologist.

records.summary: On a Norwegian locked unit, five patients and six relatives gave written accounts of network meetings and five staff joined a focus group. Participants described space for difficult perspectives. Meetings typically lasted 90 minutes with two trained facilitators. This supports asking whose voice was heard. Selected accounts cannot establish a treatment effect.

citation.authors: Lee HJ, Lin EC, Chen MB, Su TP, Chiang LC
citation.title: Randomized, controlled trial of a brief family-centred care programme for hospitalized patients with bipolar disorder and their family caregivers
citation.journal: International Journal of Mental Health Nursing

records.setting: Inpatient, one medical centre, northern Taiwan

notes: E-published December 21, 2016; the print issue is 27(1), 2018.
Both arms were invited to a routine 60-minute family discussion group; the four 90-minute sessions were in addition to it.

records.summary: A Taiwanese randomized trial involved 47 hospitalized bipolar patient–caregiver dyads. Four additional 90-minute family sessions produced favorable group-by-time differences in caregiver-reported family functioning, including communication and conflict. Caregiver burden and perceived health did not show significant interactions. A small, single-center, diagnosis-specific package cannot validate one technique.

records.group: Inpatient evidence with mixed ages and an indirect outcome

citation.authors: Haselden M, Corbeil T, Tang F, Olfson M, Dixon LB, Essock SM, Wall MM, Radigan M, Frimpong E, Wang R, Lamberti S, Schneider M, Smith TE
citation.title: Family Involvement in Psychiatric Hospitalizations: Associations With Discharge Planning and Prompt Follow-Up Care

records.design: Retrospective record review with Medicaid claims (observational)

notes: The paper also reports a 30-day outcome (OR 3.07, 95% CI 1.29–7.32); the summary above gives only the 7-day result.
The count of 31 youth could not be confirmed from the abstract or the article body; the paper defines youth as under 21, and the count is presumably in its Table 1.

records.summary: Among 179 psychiatric inpatients at two hospitals, 31 were classified as youth (20 and under). Any family–staff involvement during admission was associated with outpatient attendance within seven days of discharge (adjusted OR 2.79, 95% CI 1.28–6.08). Seven days was the outcome window. The observational design and broad definition of involvement leave relational repair unmeasured.

citation.title: The effective use of enactments in family therapy: a discovery-oriented process study
citation.journal: Journal of Marital and Family Therapy

records.summary: The authors coded 21 segments from 18 family-therapy sessions and described how a clinician initiates, facilitates and closes an exchange. This informs card 4’s sequence. It establishes neither a ward effect nor the right words for every family.

citation.authors: Miklowitz DJ, George EL, Richards JA, Simoneau TL, Suddath RL
citation.title: A randomized study of family-focused psychoeducation and pharmacotherapy in the outpatient management of bipolar disorder

notes: The comparison arm was two family-education sessions plus crisis intervention as needed. Relapse was 35% versus 54% (hazard ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.20–0.75).

records.summary: In 101 adults with bipolar disorder, 21 outpatient family-focused sessions over nine months plus medication reduced relapse versus brief family education/crisis management plus medication. A short inpatient conversation is a different exposure.

citation.authors: Rising KL, Cameron KA, Salzman DH, Papanagnou D, Doty AMB, Piserchia K, Leiby BE, Shimada A, McGaghie WC, Powell RE, Klein MR, Zhang XC, Vozenilek J, McCarthy DM
citation.title: Communicating Diagnostic Uncertainty at Emergency Department Discharge: A Simulation-Based Mastery Learning Randomized Trial

notes: Participants were resident physicians. At the first retest 52.7% of the trained group met the mastery standard versus 3.7% of the waitlist group.

records.summary: A two-site randomized study of 109 emergency clinicians tested a bundled curriculum including simulation and feedback. More intervention learners met the simulated diagnostic-uncertainty communication criterion at first retest. The bundle and outcome differ from this studio. Test transfer on an unfamiliar fictional exchange.

citation.authors: Rodolico A, Bighelli I, Avanzato C, Concerto C, Cutrufelli P, Mineo L, Schneider-Thoma J, Siafis S, Signorelli MS, Wu H, Wang D, Furukawa TA, Pitschel-Walz G, Aguglia E, Leucht S
citation.title: Family interventions for relapse prevention in schizophrenia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis

records.setting: Trials in which all patients were acutely ill were excluded
records.summary: Eleven family intervention models were compared for relapse prevention in schizophrenia. At 12 months every model except crisis-oriented interventions and family psychoeducation of two sessions or fewer reduced relapse against treatment as usual. Family psychoeducation alone had the lowest odds of relapse (OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.12–0.27). Because trials of exclusively acutely ill patients were excluded, this is an estimate for a course of family work that continues after the acute phase, not for one inpatient conversation.

citation.authors: Pharoah F, Mari J, Rathbone J, Wong W
citation.title: Family intervention for schizophrenia

records.sample: 53 randomised trials; the relapse estimate pools 32 of them (n = 2,981)
records.summary: Family intervention was associated with fewer relapses than standard care (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.5–0.6; number needed to treat 7, 95% CI 6–8). The review's authors caution that the effect may be overestimated because of the poor methodological quality of the trials.

notes: PubMed gives the DOI suffix .pub2 for this record; the Psychiatry Clerkship Library's evidence registry lists .pub3 for the same PMID. Confirm which is intended.

citation.authors: Miklowitz DJ, Efthimiou O, Furukawa TA, Scott J, McLaren R, Geddes JR, Cipriani A
citation.title: Adjunctive Psychotherapy for Bipolar Disorder: A Systematic Review and Component Network Meta-analysis

records.design: Systematic review and component network meta-analysis
records.summary: Manualised psychotherapies added to medication were associated with fewer recurrences than control treatments (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.43–0.74). Psychoeducation with guided practice of illness-management skills did better in a family or group format than the same strategies delivered individually (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.02–0.94). Family or conjoint therapy was associated with better study retention than standard psychoeducation (OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.26–0.82); its effect on depressive symptoms was uncertain.

records.group: Pooled estimates quoted in this companion

citation.authors: Ma CF, Chan SKW, Chung YL, Ng SM, Hui CLM, Suen YN, Chen EYH
citation.title: The predictive power of expressed emotion and its components in relapse of schizophrenia: a meta-analysis and meta-regression

records.setting: Cohort studies of people with schizophrenia
records.summary: High expressed emotion predicted relapse within 12 months (OR 4.87, 95% CI 3.22–7.36) more strongly than later relapse (OR 2.13, 95% CI 1.36–3.35). Critical comments predicted relapse (OR 2.22, 95% CI 1.16–4.26) and warmth was protective (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.15–0.85). These are associations from cohort studies; they describe risk, not the effect of a meeting.

records.short: HHS guidance on sharing and on listening
records.summary: Two HHS Office for Civil Rights answers on HIPAA and adult mental health information: when a provider may discuss an adult patient's information with family, and what family members can do when they are concerned.

notes: Both pages load and show “Content last reviewed September 12, 2017.”

records.summary: Maine's confidentiality statute for mental health information, including subsection 5-A on disclosure to family and caretakers; the federal rule on substance use disorder treatment records; and the Veterans Health Administration directive on family services, whose section 6.b requires private, individual screening before conjoint work.

notes: §1207 is titled “Confidentiality of information”; subsection 5-A is headed “Disclosure to family, caretakers.”
The VA document is VHA Directive 1163.04(1), Family Services in Mental Health, dated June 17, 2019 and amended March 7, 2025.
The HHS page states that compliance with the 2024 Part 2 final rule was required by February 16, 2026.

records.summary: NICE guideline CG178, Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: prevention and management (2014). It describes family intervention as a course of at least 10 planned sessions over 3 months to 1 year, delivered by competent, supervised practitioners, which can start in the acute phase, including in inpatient settings.

notes: The session count and duration are in recommendation 1.3.7.2; competence in 1.3.9.1; the offer to families and the inpatient start in 1.4.4.2.
